01 The Challenge: A lighting company cannot put its product on a shelf and expect anyone to understand it. GJAKS and its premium range MLUE sell fixtures that only make sense once they are switched on in a room. The exhibition stall design at ACE Tech Mumbai had to be a room, or several of them, with the fittings working inside.
02 What We Designed: Two timber towers hold the plot down at either end, each one a ring of curved oak fins with product shelves cut into the inside face and a chandelier hanging in the middle. A canopy sweeps between them. Walls are terracotta, with panels of artificial grass set into them so that wall lights read against something living. Inside sit a lounge with cream sofas and conifers, a brick wall behind the counter, and a mushroom-shaped timber dome over the centre.
03 Why It Worked: Terracotta and grass were chosen because almost every fitting here throws warm light, and warm light dies against white. The towers also solved a plan problem, since on three open sides there is nowhere to anchor a brand name, so the names went up on the only two vertical objects tall enough to carry them. Visitors could cross the stall between the towers without being funnelled past a counter.

title: Jaipur Furniture Exhibition Stall Design at ACE Tech Mumbai 2026
venue_name: Bombay Exhibition Centre, NESCO, Goregaon East

special_features: Rooms laid out as a bedroom, a dining and a living set | Arched niche holding a gilded deity | Carved daybed with turned balusters | Framed Rajasthani miniatures throughout | Jali screen dividing the settings
industries: Architecture, Building materials, Art and Design | Wood Industry
01 The Challenge: Jaipur Furniture by Yojna Jaisingh sells carved beds, daybeds and consoles that look wrong under trade-fair downlights on a grey carpet. Sixty square metres on a corner is enough for three rooms if nothing is wasted on circulation, so the exhibition stall design at ACE Tech Mumbai was drawn up as a house plan.
02 What We Designed: Walls were finished in textured cream plaster and broken by a deep red lacquered panel, an arched niche holding a gilded deity, and a white jali screen that divides the bedroom from the living set without closing either off. Carved corbels carry nothing and sit on the walls anyway, because that is how the furniture itself is detailed. Floors are sandstone-coloured with jute rugs, and framed Rajasthani miniatures hang at eye level throughout.
03 Why It Worked: Selling rooms works better than selling pieces for furniture like this, because a carved daybed makes no sense beside a neighbour's aluminium window system. The mandir niche is the element that reads from the aisle, since it is the one thing in the set a visitor already has at home. On a 60 sqm stall the restraint was in what was left out, mainly any signage above waist height.

title: INIT Exhibition Stall Design at ORGATEC India Mumbai 2026
design_style: Blush perimeter wall opening into furnished rooms
materials_used: Blush rendered wall planes | Sheer curtain openings | White sail canopies on slender poles | LED video wall | Upholstered acoustic wall tiles | Suspended ceiling tile panels | Grey carpet and timber flooring
special_features: Walk-through sequence of furnished offices | Acoustic panel wall in a colour patchwork | Sail canopies floating over the plot | Backlit brand panel at the corner | Ceiling tile samples hung on a tilt
industries: Architecture, Building materials, Art and Design | Manufacturing
01 The Challenge: INIT has been making workspace furniture since 1996, and brought a catalogue that runs from task chairs to acoustic ceilings. On 216 sqm open on four sides, the exhibition stall design at ORGATEC India Mumbai had to show that range as rooms somebody could walk through and sit down in.
02 What We Designed: A blush rendered wall runs the whole perimeter and is cut by openings hung with sheer curtain, each one leading into a finished room: a boardroom, a director's cabin, a meeting room, a lounge. White sail canopies float over the plot on slender poles. One wall is given over to acoustic tiles in a patchwork of weaves and reliefs under the line Makes Sound Sense, and ceiling panels hang on a tilt so visitors can see the face.
03 Why It Worked: The curtained openings are what make 216 sqm feel private. An island this size usually reads as one big room with furniture in it, and splitting the perimeter into doorways gave every product family a wall of its own. The acoustic patchwork is the one surface on the stall you want to put a hand on, so it sits where the two main aisles meet.
